A fun game system with an okay campaign and not very fun sandbox.

Gameplay revolves around building up a city (production buildings and defenses) to defeat an enemy base.

What really sets it apart is that while you have control over your own character, the rest of the citizenry has a mind of its own.

If they want armor, they'll build a forge. If they need food they'll go cook some. They'll even build defensive towers. Full 100% autonomy with no limitations. You don't get to plan out every building and action, the NPCs are largely making their own decisions.

The tradeoff is less control and sometimes NPC actions would compete with your preferred resource use, but overall it really made it feel like I was in a world of actual people, which I really enjoyed.

You do still have heavy influence on your town's progression, for example if you start a big/expensive project the NPCs will work on finishing it, and you can build extras of resource generation buildings to encourage that type of output.

Unfortunately the game doesn't do a whole lot with this. The campaign was fine, putting you through various scenarios with various challenges, and it was a nice introduction to the games' tech progression and combat strategies. Sometimes it felt a little repetitive but overall I enjoyed it.

Sandbox mode is where the game really came up short in my opinion. The inability to recruit more people made things feel very limited, and fighting AI didn't feel very satisfying since they basically were towns just like yours minus a human character guiding/pushing them forward.

I think this type of system could be really fun and chaotic if thrown into a more dynamic living world: NPCs with unlimited autonomy populating a city the human character influences and contributes to without direct control, in a world of similar cities, with populations and borders that could fluctuate at will.

The concept of this game is great and I enjoyed playing the campaign but overall it feels like a cool idea in search of a world to live in. If you want a few hours of fun experiencing that sort of unfulfilled potential, then I cautiously recommend this game.

It's a very strange take on the genre.  The concept is, theoretically, a city-builder.

The core gimmick in the game is that your allies/townspeople can, and will, autonomously do anything you can do.  That includes planting, harvesting, and building- but also, placing buildings.  There isn't really a base design aspect to this game, because a couple dozen AIs are running around slapping buildings down everywhere.  That's somewhat counteracted by the fact that every economy building in the game, like saw benches, stonecutting tables, smelters, all have fairly low durability, cannot be repaired, and simply vanish after a certain number of operations.  To the extent that you build a city, you're really just re-building those work stations to help the AI along.

You cannot give orders or priorities to your townspeople- they are well and truly autonomous, and they don't share their inventory.  You, and each of them, are on your own individual quest to gather food, build weapons, train your skills, and fight enemies, only incidentally assisting each other by proximity and shared buildings.  (Get used to them "using up" the building you're working at, forcing you to build/switch to a new one.)

All resources, including metal and stone, are "planted" in the ground by placing mana, and a few moments later they spawn. This is kinda neat.  The AI is fully capable of this, too, and so they will plant everything, everywhere.  They harvest quick though, so again, the clutter never gets wildly out of control.

There's a practice based skills system in this game, which is maybe its biggest strength, as literally every activity you do will level your stats and skills.  That feels fun, and like there's progress to be made, but.. it never quite pans out.

The truth is, you're just one guy out of 20+.  The campaign pretty much plays itself- having completed it, I'm not convinced that I was ever crucial to the map completing at any point (except one map that had some non-combat objectives on the map that the AI ignored).  Several maps I "won" while I was busily sitting at home farming and leveling skills, the enemy waves crashing on the walls and being slaughtered by my dutiful townspeople, and the defensive towers and golems they built, and the mercenary units they recruited, without any interaction from me.  

The game is a cool CRPG stapled to a cool simulation toy, and unfortunately, the ill-fitting combo makes both sides lesser.  I can't recommend the game unless you're maybe a game designer interested in seeing a game with interesting mechanics, executed decently, that doesn't come together into something coherent at the end.  I'd really like to see what the developer makes next though.

Это некий гибрид стратегии непрямого контроля, РПГ, башенной защиты и немного - симулятора выживания.
В начале мы создаём персонажа. Или двух. Или 10. Да сколько угодно. В кампании мы ограничены только одним героем. А вот в других режимах можно выбрать до 9ти персонажей. Один из них будет главным, а остальные - помощниками. Впрочем, от главаря по сути своей они ничем не отличаются. На них можно переключаться, их можно выделять рамкой. А ещё их можно отдать под управление ИИ. Который, к слову, можно тонко настраивать. Или выбрать один из готовых архетипов: лучник, маг, шахтер, плотник и тд.
Можно сделать из помощников устрашающую личную гвардию. Или же рабов, которые будут добывать ресурсы для главного героя.
Вариантов почти бесконечное количество.
Игровых режимов 2: схватка и выживание. В "Выживании" мы отстраиваем город и защищаем его от наступающих орд Тёмных Сил.
В "схватке" - сражаемся против городов ИИ, которые точно также отстраиваются и развиваются.
В игре предусмотрена смена эпох, как в Цивилизации или Age of Empires. Начинается всё в каменном веке, а заканчивается в эпохе победившего стимпанка.
Под нашим прямым управлением находится только ГГ и его помощники. Остальные горожане делают что хотят. Строят ненужные вам здания, размещают защитные башни в совершенно ненужных местах. Впрочем, я немного утрирую.
К тому же ИИ горожанам можно тонко намекать, какая постройка необходима в данный момент. Стоит лишь начать её строить, а потом оставить недостроенный остов. Какой-нибудь ушлый поселенец обязательно достроит ваше здание. Возможно не сразу, правда. Таким нехитрым способом можно экономить ресурсы. Которые, кстати, добываются довольно медленно. Добывать их может наш ГГ и его спутники. Причем у каждого есть свой инвентарь.
Прочие поселенцы тоже их добывают, но исключительно для личных нужд.
А ещё практически любое действие прокачивает соответствующий навык, начиная от размахивания булавой, и заканчивая металлургией, умением наездника, и скиллами ношения штанов и обуви.
С военными действиями похожая система: ИИ поселенцы по сути могут только отражать нападения.

[h1]+Pros+[/h1]

+Interesting Concept
+16 mission campaign
+Customize your character in true fashion
+Co-op Mode
+Semi-autonomous

[h1]-Cons-[/h1]

-Weak AI
-Camera and UI need polishing
-More maps for skirmish
-Mod support would make this game shine


[h1]The Concept:[/h1]

I really enjoy the concept of this game. You can make any character you want - whether it is a wizard, a knight, an archer, or the mixture of them all. Want to be a battlemage? Check. Want to me a gunslinger? Check. Want to kill your enemies with a rocket launcher? Oh, yes. Check. You’ll give the character the standard creation (e.g. name, gender, face, clothing, etc.) and then you have the skills/attributes that come along when you partake in a particular action or activity. Let’s say you want your character to become a knight. Well, you make a weapon, find an enemy, and attack away. You’ll level up your stats in melee. Want to progress in magic? Learn some spells and bombard your enemies.

The other interesting concept of this game is the fact that this game is somewhat autonomous. Basically, you gather your own resources – anything from wood, to metals, to food types; as well make your own equipment. While this is all happening you’ll gain stats in farming, mining, baking, etc. Now, while you’re doing this on your own, your village members will be doing the same. They’ll make their own house, gear, food, etc. You can set up the buildings for them to contribute to achieving that goal, or you can do it all on your own. They’ll also place down buildings that they deem is necessary for the village at that particular time – such as a tower for defense or a shaman hut to make ointments. You cannot, however, control the village people. They’ are left to their own devices.

[h1]The AI:[/h1]

This is where the weak AI comes into play. Some of these village people are village idiots. They’ll do their own thing by themselves and attack a fully defended base on their own and then proceed to get killed – losing most of the items on them. Yes, one can resurrect them at a shrine or church, but that defeats the purpose especially if you’re hoping for most of your villagers to coordinate a solid attack on the enemies. 

At times they’ll also just stand around and do nothing. You have the ability to grow resources – which will grow into a tree, an animal, or a metal. They too, have this ability and it isn’t used as often as one would like especially if you’re under constant threat from multiple enemies. There is also a lot of retreating. Fancy Pants decides to attack the enemy only to run away, heal up, and repeat this notion a few dozen more times. Instead of being a contributor to the village, they want to play hanky-panky with his neighbors. 

[h1]The Story:[/h1]

The campaign explains about the lore, history, and the current turmoil that is happening; it’s your job to save the denizens of this world. This title adds a lot of references from other games and places them in here as units, buildings, or even villains/heroes. I’ve seen an enemy that is well known in a particular shooter, or a certain building that is homage to an older RTS game (I won’t spoil it, but you’ll see and be like – nice!). The campaign starts off easy and then progresses to become more difficult than the last mission – maybe homage to the older RTS games? Either way, the campaign was a fun experience and the story was delightful. 

[h1]The Unpolished: [/h1]

Honestly, there isn’t a lot of gripe towards this game, but they do take the biggest hits. The UI is not so friendly towards the player. For example, if you make multiple characters that are not of the village people, you can hardly see which one you’ll have clicked. There is a tab feature that brings up all the characters you made, but it doesn’t allow you cycle through them or allow you to see if you clicked that one correctly. There is an auto mode for your characters, but remember they’ll fall under the game’s AI and may just send them to their deaths.

The other thing that was frustrating was the camera. There was no speed increase when one would pan the camera, but you could pan very slowly, or use the middle mouse button which would also forward or back out your view. Honestly, if there was a pan camera speed for when one would use the cursor against the edge of the screen it wouldn’t even be a camera issue. Unfortunately, the current camera is just not finished. 

Also, there is only one Skirmish map. You’ll play the same map over… and over… and over. No objectives, no other modes, no nothing. I think if there were more options in terms of skirmishes and way more maps the game would do better in this department as well. 

Also, if there was a mod support for this game, it would be fantastic, but there is not.

[h1]Verdict:[/h1]

Overall, a great concept and an enjoyable game that needs some polishing here and there. With a one man dev team (as far as I know) and a game that plays smooth for the most part, I would recommend as full price purchase. You’ll definitely get your money’s worth.

Have to say that right now, I'm neutral leaning towards positive about this game.

The big cons are, in my opinion:
*It's very much a grindfest. Skills are "learn by doing", with a few skills cross-linked.
*The campaign - which is supposed to double up as a tutorial - is very poor at teaching you what needs to be done.

Further adding to the grindfest is that your inventory is entirely yours, the other villages are effectively identical to players except they are AI controlled. I'd prefer it if they behaved more like servants, collecting raw materials (e.g. rocks, wood) and producing the intermediate materials (e.g. planks, cut stone), depositing said items in the warehouse (Town Hall).

Having got the bad points out the way, the rest is positive.

*You have permanent player characters that you can develop as you see fit.
*Your inventory does carry over from mission to mission
*All friendly NPCs will join in on big building projects
*There's a large quantity of items available, higher tier giving better bonuses.

Jeu mêlant RTS et RPG, Aurora Dusk est la suite de Vendetta. Je citerai en exemple ici le partage des bâtiments (tous les bâtiments construits sont utilisable par la population alliée) la destruction des bâtiments au bout d'une certaine utilisation (nombre définie de création d'objets ou de ressources avant sa destruction automatique) ou bien absence de vente autre qu'au château. This game is interesting, a mix between RPG, Tower Defense and autonomous City Buildier.
It sum up like this: you and your gang of desperate have to defend from a horde (or more) of enemies, to do so you have to build a village, craft and advance to the various "ages" to get better equipment.

Pros:
- Lot of resources, weapons, armors, items... and almost everything is useful and upgradable.
- Age progression and development.
- Missions and skirmishes can easily hook you up.
- Persistent character progression. Basically you can endlessy develop your character.
- Spawnable resources with mana.
- Various races with their pros and cons, plus a lot of skills to develop.

Not good, nor terrible
- Music is nice, also the graphic if you don't zoom in too much.
- Bare-bone UI, it takes a bit to get used.
- Avatar customization. There is, essential but present.
- Some workstations have a lot to craft, others can be easily overlooked of have a age-limited use.
- Limited-use workstation. Per-se isn't bad, but npc tend to overuse them and then build in the other side of the town.

Cons:
- The npc AI. It seems to be some way to control the npc, but I didn't checked well. Leaving it unchanged, the npc AI is pure chaos: they build and spawn resources whenever they can in every possible place, charge head on and even take battle in the middle of a river. Oh, and expect random magic as they like to use it to hunt down animals.
- No village management at all. As I said, it's pure chaos.
- Clunky and limited troop control.
- No resource sharing, everyone (and the player) are on their own in gathering and crafting.
- Enemy AI isn't better (but can be pardoned if considering their ridicolous numbers).

In my opinion, the game could greatly improve if given to the player only the building organization and providing a shared resource pool, maybe with some drop-off locations or building able to spawn-generate resources.
In overall, is a nice and interesting premise with a lot of potential and a possible opening for modding in terms of adding items, buildings, enemies and scenarios/maps. 

Even with  its problems I would suggest it, if you are into the Tower Defense genre or like me want to try something interesting, but there is still work to do.
I'll give it a 7/10 with hopes for the future.

Aurora Dusk is a unique mix of real time strategy, village building simulator and RPG, where up to 200+ villagers, 200+ soldiers and 400+ monsters can exist on the map at once as the villagers build, craft and fight to survive.  It's one of the few games nowadays where I actually feel like I can both grind crafting and feel like it has a real impact in a somewhat fun to watch manner.

Crafting ranges from building melee weapons and armor to be a frontline fighter, ranged weapons like bows, crossbows, firearms and artillery (yes!), magical staffs, wands and rings which cast spells to obliterate monsters en masse, or focusing on building defenses, golems (think super soldiers built with building materials) or selling goods on the market to raise funds to raise an army.  It's rough around the edges, controls are awkward at first, the AI can by derpy at times, and it's not very impressive graphically, but I wish there were more games like this.  Hopefully it will act as inspiration for more similar games in the future and is absolutely worth the price if you enjoy crafting and can overlook the UI and graphics.
